Bread dough rises because yeast consumes sugars and releases carbon dioxide gas. A developed gluten network in the dough traps that gas. As the gas builds up, it expands the dough, making it rise. Yeast produces the gas, while gluten provides the structure that holds it in.

Temperature affects how quickly this happens. Within normal proofing temperatures, warmth generally makes yeast more active, so dough rises faster. A cool rise slows yeast activity and takes longer, but that extra time can allow more flavor to develop. More heat is not always better: excessively hot conditions can damage or kill the yeast.

Leaving dough to proof too long can also cause trouble. Its structure may weaken until it can no longer hold the gas well. The dough can then lose gas and collapse. Because recipes and conditions vary, watch the dough’s expansion and texture rather than relying only on a fixed time.
